name: PETG (Glycol-Modified PET)
chemical_makeup: Polyethylene terephthalate glycol-modified — a copolyester of PET in which cyclohexanedimethanol (CHDM) replaces part of the ethylene glycol, suppressing crystallisation to give an amorphous, tough, easily printed polymer
summary: The workhorse step up from PLA: tougher, far better layer adhesion, genuinely water-resistant and usable to ~70 °C, with only mild warp and no enclosure requirement. Pays for it with stringing, oozing, softer detail and supports that fuse hard to the part.

printing.notes: Prusa profiles run 230 °C first layer / 240 °C for the rest; the Prusament TDS quotes 250±10 °C. Keep part cooling low — fan off for the first layers, then roughly half power; heavy cooling is the main cause of brittle, poorly bonded PETG. No chamber needed, but a draft-free room (or an enclosure on large parts) helps. Hardened nozzle only for CF/GF-filled PETG.

feeding.notes: Listed AMS-compatible by Bambu and unproblematic in Prusa's MMU: rigid, non-abrasive and only moderately hygroscopic. The exception is CF/GF-filled PETG from third parties, which is barred because the fibres abrade the AMS PTFE tubes. Enclosure: Bambu's heat-creep table and QIDI's door-open table both keep the cover installed for PETG, so enclosure_open_for_cooling is false — PETG's Tg is high enough that chamber heat helps rather than hurts, though Bambu does note PETG can suffer heat creep if the enclosure runs unusually hot.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping/hissing or steam at the nozzle tip; glossy rather than foggy or matte extrudate; markedly reduced stringing; no surface bubbles or voids in the extruded strand
drying.notes: Prusa recommends 55 °C for 6 h, Bambu 65 °C for 8 h; heavily soaked spools may need 6-10 h. Do not exceed ~65-70 °C — spools deform. Wet PETG bubbles and hydrolyses visibly, so drying is effectively routine rather than occasional.

storage.recommendations: Sealed container or drybox with desiccant; re-absorbs moisture noticeably faster than PLA, so store it sealed between prints rather than only before them

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $22-26, premium $30-42 per kg. The historical price gap with ABS has closed — budget PETG now often matches or undercuts ABS.

recommended: outdoor brackets and enclosures (moderate UV exposure)
water bottles and non-potable liquid containment
parts where layer adhesion / Z-strength is critical
not_recommended: high-precision dimensional parts (more ooze and stringing than PLA)
parts with crisp overhangs or long bridges (sags and droops)
geometry needing easy support removal (supports fuse strongly)
fine-detail miniatures (glossy, stringy finish blurs detail)

properties.notes: Prusament PETG measures HDT 68 °C and yield ~46-50 MPa; Polymaker PolyLite PETG reports 50.8 MPa and partmfg.com 52.2 MPa. Tg is not on the Prusament TDS; secondary sources put it at 80-85 °C. Max service temp is an estimate, not a datasheet value. 3D-Fuel's Pro PETG TDS (technical library, read 2026-08-01) is a third manufacturer sheet but is plainly the base resin supplier's injection-moulding datasheet — 3.2 mm moulded specimens, ASTM D955 mould shrinkage, Rockwell hardness — not printed-part data, and it must be read that way. It confirms the recorded shrinkage low end exactly (0.002 mm/mm = 0.2 % parallel to flow, ASTM D955) and puts specific gravity at 1.28 against the 1.27 recorded. It adds flexural 75 MPa at 2,200 MPa modulus, notched Izod 69 J/m at 23 °C falling to 28 J/m at -40 °C with unnotched 2,600 J/m, Rockwell R106, and water absorption 0.13 % in 24 h. Two figures do not fit the recorded values: HDT 67/62 °C at 0.455/1.82 MPa, below the 72 °C recorded, and tensile 25 MPa which is a BREAK stress after 30 % drawing, not the yield strength the 40-55 MPa range is built from — the sheet gives no yield figure, so the two are not comparable. No Tg is given.

compatibility.notes: Welds cleanly to itself and to PCTG (same copolyester family); some TPU formulations bond to PETG but the weld is weaker than a same-family joint, so treat flex/rigid PETG-TPU as semi-compatible only. Does not weld to PLA — deliberately, so PLA makes a clean breakaway support for PETG and vice versa. BVOH is the soluble support of choice (PVA pairs better with PLA). PETG plus ABS/ASA is not a standard combination: the chemistry, nozzle windows and warp behaviour clash even though bed temperatures overlap.

plate_recommendations.notes: Textured/satin or powder-coated PEI is the right surface for PETG at 70-90 °C bed. On SMOOTH PEI, always apply a glue stick as a separator — bare PETG bonds so hard it can tear the coating off the sheet on removal.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Explicitly listed compatible by Prusa, and one of the quiet advantages of this sheet: no separation layer is needed, unlike smooth PEI where PETG fusing is a standing hazard.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Generally no glue needed — G10 does not develop the aggressive chemical bond PETG forms with smooth PEI or bare glass.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Prusa markets satin as an excellent PETG surface with no glue stick required — parts pop off cleanly once cold.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): A standout use case — vendors specifically call out that PETG does not bond excessively here, unlike smooth PEI or PEX where it can weld on and tear the surface.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): PETG chemically bonds to bare smooth PEI and routinely rips chunks of film out on removal. Treat the glue stick as a mandatory separator, not an adhesion aid.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): The classic glass hazard: PETG bonds chemically to bare glass and can pull a conchoidal chip out of the plate on removal. Glue stick is used here as a barrier, not for grip.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Officially supported and Bambu publishes a dedicated PETG-on-SuperTack guide, but this is the plate's most contested material: multiple forum threads report over-adhesion, torn coa

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Works, but the vendor's own wording is that it requires special print settings to avoid fusion — copolyester chemically welds to this film if the first layer is squished hard or th

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Clear and translucent PETG shows the effect well and adhesion is generally adequate, but behaviour varies by vendor coating (unverified across brands).

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Bambu explicitly warns of bubbling and sticking on the plain Cool Plate — the PC sheet is damaged, not merely over-adhered. Note that PETG IS listed as acceptable on the Cool Plate

emissions.notes: No styrene, and odour is mild. Azimi et al. (2016) placed PET-based filament (T-Glase) around 5×10⁹ particles/min — above PLA but well below ABS, PC and HIPS; a precise figure for generic PETG is unverified. Ventilation is optional for occasional open-air printing and recommended for long or enclosed jobs.

safety_notes: Carbon- and glass-filled PETG grades are abrasive and require a hardened nozzle; fibre dust from sanding filled grades should not be inhaled.
additional_notes: Base PETG resin is used for injection-moulded food packaging and some filament lines are sold as food-contact certified, but a printed part's layer crevices and unverified nozzle/additive contamination mean an FDM PETG part is not food-safe without sealing or single-use handling. PIPG ('Post-Industrial PET-G', MCPP) is ~70% recycled PETG resin sold mainly as pellets for large-format printing — chemically PETG-class, aliased here rather than a separate entry.

provenance.conflicts: HDT: Prusament measures 68 °C while other property tables cite 78-80 °C — recorded as 72 °C with the 68-80 °C spread noted. Hygroscopy: the Prusament TDS reports only 0.07-0.10 % moisture uptake at 7 days for that formulation, while field consensus classes bulk PETG as a moderate-to-high absorber needing routine drying — 'moderate' recorded. Shrinkage: some sources place PETG slightly below PLA, others slightly above. The particulate figure is extrapolated from a PET-based filament (T-Glase), not measured for generic PETG. 2026-08-01 update (3D-Fuel technical library published — owner-provided link): the Pro PETG TDS was mined and NO recorded value was changed. HDT: it measures 67 °C at 0.455 MPa, which drops below the previously noted 68-80 °C spread and lands next to Prusament's 68 °C — two datasheets now cluster near 67-68 °C against the 78-80 °C property tables, so the recorded 72 °C is looking high, but it is retained pending a fourth source. Tensile: its 25 MPa is tensile at BREAK (30 % elongation), not at yield, so it does not contradict the 40-55 MPa yield range despite appearing to; flagged because a naive merge would corrupt the range. Density 1.28 vs the recorded 1.27 is inside normal brand spread. Nozzle temperature: 3D-Fuel specifies 245-265 °C (melt 249-271 °C), above the recorded 220-250 °C window and above even Prusament's 250±10 °C — the hottest PETG guidance found. Drying: 71 °C for 4-6 h exceeds the recorded 50-65 °C ceiling, but that is pellet drying on a resin datasheet, not spool drying, and should not be applied to a wound spool. Water absorption 0.13 % in 24 h (ASTM D570) sits above Prusament's 0.07-0.10 % at 7 days, mildly supporting the 'moderate' hygroscopy class rather than Prusament's low figure. Shrinkage 0.2 % confirms the recorded band's low end.
